reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because its ordinary Coinbase wallet tutorial is paired with a direct solicitation for paid mining-pool participation, telling viewers to click an external link and join as a member. The description claims that a $600 mining-pool investment produced over $3,000 in two months and calls it "Very easy money and profitable," while the speaker says he is focused on Bitcoin mining and will provide a link to what he does.

opening.argument: Judge the speaker's guidance alongside the promotional description. He cautions viewers about keeping money in an online wallet and recommends considering other wallets, rather than presenting cryptocurrency use as risk-free. He also describes his Coinbase account as new and his demonstration as a quick account walkthrough. The description's mining earnings are a first-person claim, not a promise that viewers will receive the same return. That distinction matters when deciding whether the video is primarily deceptive solicitation or a tutorial that includes the creator's personal experience.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited $600-to-$3,000 statement is a claimed personal result, not an explicit guarantee of anyone else's earnings. The description does urge a click and says membership is required, but the speaker's closing also cautions against concentrating money in the online wallet. Those qualifications do not erase the promotion; they do make the opening's characterization of the whole video as an unqualified earnings pitch too broad.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The warning concerns storage in an online wallet, not the mining offer. It does not qualify the description's invitation to click, join a mining pool as a member, and associate a $600 investment with more than $3,000 in two months. The speaker also directs interested viewers to the description for the mining activity. A lack of an explicit guarantee does not neutralize that paid-participation earnings pitch.

opening.argument: The video teaches a concrete wallet workflow. The speaker begins by saying he will show Coinbase, explains account creation and phone verification, then shows how to find a receiving address and describes a small transfer from another wallet. He also walks through settings and two-factor security. That operational detail is the substance of the presentation. His later mention of a mining link is brief in the spoken walkthrough; it does not turn the demonstrated account setup, wallet receipt, and security steps into instructions for joining a mining pool.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly identifies the description's mining pitch, but it leaves out how much of the spoken material is devoted to ordinary wallet operations. The speaker's invitation to see what he does in mining comes after the account walkthrough. The $600 and earnings claim appears in the description; it is not a step he demonstrates while showing viewers how to create and use the wallet. The tutorial remains the stronger reading of the video itself.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The wallet instructions are real, but they do not make the attached solicitation incidental. The speaker explicitly sends viewers to the description for his mining activity. There, the text tells them to click the link, says joining requires membership, and presents unusually easy earnings from a $600 investment. A tutorial can supply the setting for a separate paid-mining pitch.

opening.argument: The clearest incentive the speaker explains in the walkthrough is an ordinary invite-friends offer tied to someone spending over $100 on Coinbase. He describes a shareable link, not a chain of recruits or a promised investment return. The mining description is more promotional, but its $600 and earnings figures are framed as the creator's own experience; the supplied material does not show the linked pool's payment process, a demand for credentials, or a guaranteed return for viewers. The evidence supports recognizing promotion without assuming those unshown mechanisms.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening combines two distinct offers. The spoken $10 invite reward concerns a Coinbase referral after a friend spends over $100; it is not evidence of returns from the mining pool. The description's first-person earnings claim deserves scrutiny, but it does not show what a viewer must pay, whether anyone else receives those returns, or a downline-income arrangement. Those missing details limit what can be concluded about the external service from this record.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The Coinbase referral is ordinary, but it is not the disputed offer. The description separately directs viewers to click a mining link, says they must become a member to join, and promotes an investment said to have earned over $3,000 in two months as easy money. The speaker connects that offer to the video by promising a link to his mining activity. The record need not display the external checkout or a downline to establish what the video promotes.
